prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute post-stroke cognitive impairment to depression without formal assessment
Do not read the chronic petechial haemorrhagic transformation as a new haemorrhage and stop the antiplatelet
Do not defer secondary prevention until cognition is 'settled' — recurrent stroke is the main risk to cognition
Do not certify fitness to drive on the strength of motor recovery when attentional neglect is documented
Do not prescribe anticholinergic or sedating medications during cognitive rehabilitation
required_recommendations: Screen cognition after stroke rather than assuming that motor recovery represents recovery
Establish the temporal relationship: onset within three months of a documented stroke satisfies the NINDS-AIREN criterion
Distinguish post-stroke cognitive impairment from post-stroke depression with formal scales
Document the deficit and its functional consequence with an informant-rated scale to place it at the dementia threshold
Obtain MRI and relate the cognitive profile to the infarct territory and the pre-existing small-vessel burden
Intensify secondary prevention, since recurrent stroke is the main determinant of further decline
Refer for cognitive rehabilitation and complete the driving assessment; plan reassessment because the trajectory can still change

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG has no diagnostic role in vascular cognitive impairment; it belongs to the differential of a rapidly progressive or fluctuating course (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, non-convulsive status, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy), none of which is present here

A presynaptic dopaminergic study answers the Lewy-body question, not the vascular one, and there is no spontaneous parkinsonism, no fluctuating cognition with hallucinations and no REM sleep behaviour disorder
Cardiac sympathetic imaging is a test for dementia with Lewy bodies and for autonomic failure; it says nothing about cerebrovascular disease

An untargeted paraneoplastic or autoimmune-encephalitis battery in a chronic stepwise decline with a hypertensive imaging burden is the archetypal expensive miss; the indication for those assays is a subacute multidomain syndrome
The MRI already obtained answers everything a CT could and more: CT cannot show microbleeds or cortical superficial siderosis, so it cannot grade the vascular burden this diagnosis rests on
There is no embolic lesion pattern to explain: the burden here is small-vessel, and a structural cardioembolic source would not account for it
Prolonged rhythm monitoring is for an unexplained embolic infarct pattern; in pure small-vessel disease it changes nothing about the diagnosis or the treatment

accepted: Post-stroke vascular dementia following a right middle cerebral artery superior division infarct, on a background of pre-existing moderate small-vessel disease

differential.key_features: Common at ten weeks and a genuine confounder, but he denies low mood, the Geriatric Depression Scale is 4/15, he engages with rehabilitation, and the deficit is attentional and executive with objective left-sided inattention
Alertness is stable with no fluctuation, no new medication and no infective or metabolic trigger

differential.diagnosis: Alzheimer's disease unmasked by the stroke
differential.key_features: There is no premorbid history of cognitive decline, the hippocampi are preserved, and recall is cue-responsive; a biomarker would be required to raise this and nothing in the presentation calls for it

differential.diagnosis: Expected early post-stroke cognitive recovery trajectory
differential.key_features: Cognitive deficits at ten weeks may still improve, which is why the diagnosis is dated from the event and reassessed — but the functional impairment now is real and requires management now
No fluctuation, hallucinations, spontaneous parkinsonism or dream enactment

key_clinical_evidence: Post-stroke dementia is diagnosed on the temporal criterion: cognitive decline beginning within three months of a documented stroke, with a deficit that the lesion can explain
Motor and cognitive recovery dissociate after stroke, and a good NIHSS improvement says nothing about executive function
Pre-existing small-vessel disease lowers cognitive reserve and helps explain why a single infarct produced a dementia in this patient
Chronic petechial haemorrhagic transformation after thrombolysis is expected and is not a reason to withdraw antiplatelet therapy
Cognitive deficits at ten weeks can still evolve, so the diagnosis carries a reassessment plan rather than being treated as fixed

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Pietro Lombardi is a 75-year-old retired site manager who had a right middle cerebral artery infarct ten weeks ago, thrombolysed with a fall in NIHSS from 12 to 3. His motor recovery has been good: he walks with a stick and uses the left hand for gross tasks. His wife's concern is different. Since discharge he has not been able to resume anything requiring organisation: he cannot follow the sequence of his own medication, has twice set out for the pharmacy and returned without going in, and cannot manage the household bills he handled until the day of the stroke. He loses the thread of a conversation with two other people present, misses objects on his left in the kitchen, and does not seem fully aware of the extent of his difficulties. He remembers events when reminded of the context. There has been slow improvement in the motor deficit over ten weeks with no corresponding improvement in the organisational difficulty. He denies low mood, sleeps adequately and engages with rehabilitation willingly. There are no hallucinations, no fluctuation in alertness and no dream enactment. His blood pressure at discharge and since has been in the 145-155 range and his HbA1c is 7.9%.

neurological_exam.additional: Pulse regular at 78. No carotid bruit. No tremor. Mood reactive, denies persistent low mood.

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive. Extraocular movements full, mild gaze preference to the right on distraction. Left homonymous inattention without a field cut on formal confrontation. Left nasolabial flattening.
neurological_exam.gait: Hemiparetic with circumduction of the left leg, using a stick. No falls since discharge.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person and place, year correct, month incorrect. MoCA 20/30 with losses in trail-making, cube, clock, digit span backwards, serial sevens and delayed recall (3/5 unaided, 5/5 cued). Mild left-sided inattention on cancellation (3 omissions). Insight into the deficits is partial.

neurological_exam.reflexes: 3+ on the left, 2+ on the right, left plantar extensor.
neurological_exam.sensory: Reduced light touch and graphaesthesia on the left; extinction on double simultaneous stimulation.
